title: Gold aureus of Claudius, minted at Rome in 41–42 CE, found in India — and cut through the emperor's head with a chisel
language_note:
British Museum catalog record in English, and — unlike `persia-03-coin`, whose `language_note` complains that the BM does not transcribe its Pahlavi legends — this record's museum DOES transcribe the coin's own Latin, so the excerpt carries it.

THE RECORD DECLARES TWO LANGUAGES AND THE INDEX WILL SEE ONE, AND THAT IS FINDING 86 SHOWING UP HARMLESSLY. `classify_original` forces `object_description` on any FIND_TYPES record and then sets `lang` to the declared primary only when `non_latin_ratio >= 0.30`; Latin is Latin script, so the chunk is declared `en` whatever this field says. Here that costs nothing — the span is mostly English curatorial prose and the two Latin strings are twenty-eight and twenty-five characters. On a Thai or a French description the same branch costs a record, which is what FINDING 86 is about.
date: Production date 41-42, as the British Museum records it. Claudius's second year, and the coin traveled to India within the generation that the Periplus describes.
findspot: `Excavated/Findspot: India (historic - pre-1947) (probably)` — the British Museum's own words, hedge included. NO SITE IS NAMED. The coin was `Donated by: HH Raja Martanda Tondaiman, Raja of Pudukkottai` in 1898, and Pudukkottai in Tamil Nadu is where the Raja's gift came from; but the museum records the findspot as India and does not say Pudukkottai, so this record does not say it either. A donor's title is not a findspot.

findspot_places.name: India — the British Museum's findspot, hedged by the museum as `(probably)`
findspot_places.note: NO ID, AND THE HEDGE IS THE MUSEUM'S. The field reads `India (historic - pre-1947) (probably)`; a subcontinent with a parenthetical doubt on it is exactly what `regional` is for, and a gazetteer id here would turn a museum's hedge into a coordinate. THE OBVIOUS TEMPTATION WAS PUDUKKOTTAI and it is refused: the donor was the Raja of Pudukkottai and the 1898,0803 series is his gift, but the BM's findspot field does not name the town and this corpus does not upgrade a provenance into a findspot. `africa-02-aksumite-coin` refused Pleiades 39269 for Aden on the same principle — a resolving id at the wrong place is worse than no id.

origin_places.name: Rome — the mint, as the British Museum states it
origin_places.note:
`stated` because the museum's `Production place` field reads `Minted in: Rome (city)`, with its own hierarchy spelled out beneath it — `Europe: Italy: Lazio: Rome (province): Rome (city)`. THIS IS THE ONE CASE WHERE THIS CORPUS MAY TAKE PLEIADES 423025, AND IT IS WORTH SAYING WHY. The standing rule is `do not import Pleiades 423025 Roma for a text that names the Roman state` — `kēsar`, `Hrōmāy`, `walhakurn`, `mlk Rmn` and `mlk Frs¹` have all been refused an id on it, because a people, a state, an office and a title are not settlements. Here the source names the CITY, distinguishes it from the province in the same breath, and names it as the place where a physical object was struck. That is a settlement doing what settlements do. Confirmed in this session against the cached 2026-08-10 snapshot: title `Roma`, description `The capital of the Roman Republic and Empire.`, repr_point 12.491/41.890, feature types `urban, settlement`, `location_precision` `related`, -750..2100.

AND THE TWO BLOCKS ARE THE POINT OF THE RECORD. Minted at Rome, found in India, and the map draws the line between them.

original_text_note:
FOUR VALUES FROM THE BRITISH MUSEUM'S RECORD, ASSEMBLED IN A DECLARED ORDER, AND THE ASSEMBLY IS AN EDITORIAL ACT THAT IS DIGESTED RATHER THAN TRUSTED. In order: the whole of the `Description` field (three lines, as the museum breaks them); the `Inscription content` for the obverse; the `Inscription content` for the reverse; and the whole of `Curator's comments`. Joined by single newlines. Nothing else, and not one word of this project's prose — the museum's field LABELS are not carried, because they are the page's furniture rather than its content.

VERIFIED BY DIGEST ACROSS TWO MACHINES, over the RESULT of the assembly and not over the parts. The same four values were sliced out of the live page in the browser by field boundaries and joined by the same rule; the same four were typed on the bridge and joined by the same rule; SHA-256 was computed on both and compared. `eastasia-08-songshi-fulin` established this in F6 for an EDIT — Kanripo's `¶` and `<pb:...>` markers stripped by the same two rules on both machines — and an assembly is the same act with the pieces the other way round. The editorial step is the part a curator's eye is worst at checking, and it is the part that is checked.

    chars 183   sha256 0740202da25683267f16e04156e96fcecee42f2fed87dcbb8c23b07951481e04

No non-breaking space and no double space anywhere in it.

WHY THE CURATOR'S COMMENT IS IN THE EXCERPT AND NOT IN `notes`. `Vertical chisel-cut on head.` is five words and it is the entire reason this coin was taken rather than any of the seventy-four others the British Museum holds under `Turner 1989 / Roman Coins from India`. A field the loader does not chunk is a field the model never sees, which is the trap `what_gloss_capable_MEANS_mechanically` exists to name; the same trap catches a record whose one interesting sentence is filed where nothing can retrieve it.

citation_original:
THE POSITION IS `all_rights_reserved`, AND IT IS NOT THE FLATTERING READING THAT WAS AVAILABLE.

The object page states one thing about rights and it is a bare notice, read off https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/C_1898-0803-11 on 2026-09-06:

"© 2026 The Trustees of the British Museum"

WHAT THE MUSEUM SAYS ELSEWHERE, AND WHY IT DOES NOT APPLY HERE. https://www.britishmuseum.org/terms-use/copyright-and-permissions says the Museum "increasingly intend[s] to release content on our website under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) licence" — and, in the next breath, that "The Creative Commons licence does not apply to everything on our website. Content that is published under the Creative Commons licence will be marked with the following logo".

THE MARKING WAS LOOKED FOR AND IS NOT THERE. The rendered page was searched on 2026-09-06 for the string `Creative Commons`, for the string `CC BY`, and for any anchor whose href contains `creativecommons`: zero of each, in the whole document and not only in the visible text. One copyright line, no licence badge. So the licence the Museum intends for SOME of its content is not asserted over this record, and the honest position is the one the page actually states.

THIS IS THE SECOND RIGHTS CELL IN THIS TRANCHE WHERE THE ADVERTISED READING WAS WRONG, IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS. On `arabia-08-walters-marib-pediment` the object page's CC0 badge covers the images and NOT the text this corpus takes (FINDING 87). Here a site-level CC BY-NC-SA intent covers marked content and this record is not marked. FINDING 69 was produced by two licence claims wrong in opposite directions in a single session; ruling 74's column exists so that the direction of each error is recorded rather than averaged.

WHAT `all_rights_reserved` DOES AND DOES NOT MEAN HERE. It is a statement about what the SOURCE said, not a verdict on whether 183 characters of catalogue description may be quoted in a research corpus. The column is `COUNTED, NOT GATED`. Nothing in this repository refuses a record on its rights position and this record is not asking for an exception.
notes:
F7's South Asia `catalogue_record` slot. Third record of the tranche, fiftieth in the corpus.

WHY THIS COIN OUT OF SEVENTY-FIVE. The British Museum's bibliography term for `Turner 1989 / Roman Coins from India` lists seventy-five objects — every Roman coin in the collection with an Indian findspot, including the whole 1898,0803 series the Raja of Pudukkottai gave. Most of them are bullion: an aureus, a weight, a findspot, and nothing else to say. This one has five words of curator's comment that turn it into an event. `Vertical chisel-cut on head.` A Julio-Claudian gold coin is carried to South India by the Red Sea trade — the trade `southasia-02-periplus-muziris` and `southasia-03-muziris-papyrus` document from the Roman end — and then somebody in India puts a chisel through the emperor's face. The British Museum exhibited it in 2016-17 under the title `Defacing the past: desecration and damnation in imperial Rome`.

WHAT IT ADDS THAT SOUTH ASIA DID NOT HAVE. The corpus's South Asian records are two Roman-world texts about the Malabar trade, a Tamil poem, a Sanskrit astronomical text, and an excavation summary of Pattanam. Every one of them is a DOCUMENT. This is the region's first Roman OBJECT, and it is one whose interest lies in what was done to it after it arrived. `southasia-04-pattanam` records that Roman material reaches India; this records that it was then handled, and not reverently.

AND THE LEGEND IS WORTH THE TWENTY-FIVE CHARACTERS. `EX.S.C. OB CIVES SERVATOS` — by decree of the Senate, for having saved the citizens — is an oak-wreath legend about the emperor as saviour of Roman citizens, on a coin that ended its life in India with a chisel through the portrait. The corpus holds the Roman state's own self-description and its reception beyond the empire on the same 183-character chunk, which is not an argument this record makes anywhere in its prose and does not need to.

MINTED AT ROME AND FOUND IN INDIA: the two place blocks are the record. It is also the only object in this corpus that may take Pleiades 423025 — see `origin_places` for why the standing refusal does not apply.

RULING 79's P4 PREDICTS THIS RECORD CROWDS NOTHING. It is 183 characters, the shortest excerpt in the corpus, and P4 says at most two of F7's five catalogue records appear in any `beaten_by` list in the run. This is the record most likely to appear in none.
